items.title: Why Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz runs through Qeshm
items.hook: The US struck Iranian air defences on Qeshm Island on 6 Nov, its second strike there in a week. The island sits at the heart of a strategy Iran built after its naval clashes with the US in the 1980s [[e:Tanker War]].
items.body:
Look at a map and Iran's advantage is obvious. The Strait of Hormuz is only about 35 miles wide at its narrowest, and its northern shore, along with a chain of islands led by **Qeshm**, the largest island in the Gulf, belongs to Iran. Whoever holds those shores can watch, and threaten, every tanker leaving the Gulf. Empires understood this long before oil: the Portuguese seized Hormuz island in the early 1500s, and Persia's Shah Abbas, with English ships, drove them out in the [[e:Capture of Ormuz (1622)|1622 capture of Ormuz]].

The modern story begins with Britain's exit. When London withdrew its forces from the Gulf in 1971, the Shah moved to fill the gap. On the eve of the UAE's founding, Iran took the Greater and Lesser Tunbs by force and Abu Musa under a deal with Sharjah, in the [[e:Seizure of Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs|seizure of the three islands]]. The UAE has disputed them ever since. Iran now held a ring of positions across the shipping lanes.

The 1979 revolution turned that geography against the West, and the [[e:Iran–Iraq War]] {{note: Started when Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980; it ended in a UN-brokered ceasefire in August 1988.}} showed how it could be used. From 1984 Iraq attacked tankers carrying Iranian oil, and Iran hit back at ships serving Iraq's Gulf backers, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. In this [[e:Tanker War]] some 450 ships were struck. In 1987 Washington agreed to fly the US flag on Kuwaiti tankers and escort them, in [[e:Operation Earnest Will]]. Iran answered with mines and speedboats run by the [[p:Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps]]. {{note: Created by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's decree in May 1979 to defend the revolution, alongside Iran's regular military.}}

The turning point came in April 1988. A mine nearly sank the frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts, and four days later the US Navy struck back in [[e:Operation Praying Mantis]], sinking much of Iran's regular navy in a single day. That July, the cruiser USS Vincennes mistook a passenger jet for an attacker and shot down [[e:Iran Air Flight 655]], killing all 290 aboard. Iran accepted a ceasefire weeks later.

Tehran drew a lasting lesson: it could not win a ship-against-ship battle with America, but it could make the strait too dangerous to use. Over the following decades the [[p:Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy|Guards' navy]] built up mines, fast attack craft and anti-ship missiles, many dug into tunnels on islands like Qeshm, and took the lead role in the strait. It seized tankers in the 2019 crisis to show it could.

The 2026 war tested that strategy for real. After US–Israeli strikes began on 28 February, Iran shut the strait, and Washington answered with the [[e:2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|naval blockade of Iran]]. The new US strikes on Qeshm's air defences hit the core of the system Iran spent 35 years building, which is why each one risks wider fighting even as both sides talk.

timeline.text: Safavid Persia and the English East India Company expel the Portuguese from Hormuz island.
As Britain leaves the Gulf, Iran takes Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs; the UAE still claims them.
The [[e:Tanker War]] begins inside the Iran–Iraq War; some 450 ships are hit by 1988.
The US begins escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in [[e:Operation Earnest Will]].
After a mine hits USS Samuel B. Roberts, [[e:Operation Praying Mantis]] sinks much of Iran's regular navy.
USS Vincennes shoots down [[e:Iran Air Flight 655]], killing 290; Iran accepts a ceasefire weeks later.
War begins on 28 Feb; Iran closes the strait and the US imposes a [[e:2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|naval blockade]].
US strikes hit air defences on Qeshm on 2 and 6 Nov while indirect talks continue.

perspectives.view: Tehran tells this as a story of foreign powers, from the Portuguese to the US Navy, trying to dominate waters on its doorstep. It sees control of the strait as legitimate self-defence and its only real leverage against a stronger enemy and its blockade.
Washington frames its role since 1987 as protecting freedom of navigation for the world's oil supply. It casts mining and tanker attacks as illegal threats to neutral shipping that it must deter.

The UAE describes the 1971 island takeover as an occupation of its territory on the eve of independence. Gulf states want the strait open but fear being caught in a US–Iran war fought along their coasts.

keyTerms.meaning: Iran's largest island, lying along the strait's northern side; it hosts Revolutionary Guard naval and air-defence sites.
The Revolutionary Guards' naval force, built around mines, fast boats and coastal missiles, which leads Iran's operations in the strait.
Registering foreign ships under a country's flag so its navy can protect them, as the US did for Kuwaiti tankers in 1987.
The principle that ships may pass through international straits; the US invokes it, while Iran disputes how it applies in the 2026 war.

items.whyItMatters: Iran's whole Hormuz strategy rests on islands like Qeshm, so US strikes there weaken Tehran's main bargaining chip and also risk a wider fight. The 1988 record shows such clashes can escalate fast, and one mistake can kill civilians. Watch whether the Qatari-mediated sequence of steps reopens the strait before more strikes hit the islands.

items.recallQ: Why did Iran build its naval strategy in the strait around mines, fast boats and island missile sites rather than a large conventional fleet?
items.recallA: In April 1988, Operation Praying Mantis showed that Iran's regular navy could not survive a direct fight with the US Navy. The Revolutionary Guards concluded that cheap, scattered, hard-to-hit weapons could make the strait too dangerous to use, giving Iran leverage without winning a sea battle.

items.title: How Serbia's students ended the Vučić era
items.hook: Final results confirmed on 5 Nov that the Student List won a clear majority in Serbia's parliament, ending more than a decade of [[p:Aleksandar Vučić]]'s dominance. It is the second time in 26 years that a student-led movement has brought down a Serbian strongman, and the first did not end the way its heroes hoped.
items.body:
Serbia has toppled a strongman with students in the streets once before. In the late 1990s [[p:Slobodan Milošević]] ruled a country battered by the [[e:Yugoslav Wars]], sanctions and hyperinflation. A dozen students in Belgrade founded [[p:Otpor]], {{note: Founded in Belgrade on 10 October 1998 by a small group of students, using a clenched-fist logo and street humour against Milošević.}} a leaderless movement built on mockery, discipline and nonviolence. When Milošević tried to deny [[p:Vojislav Koštunica]] victory in the September 2000 presidential vote, hundreds of thousands converged on Belgrade, and on 5 October he fell in the [[e:Overthrow of Slobodan Milošević|Bulldozer Revolution]].

The democrats who replaced him disappointed many. Reformist prime minister [[p:Zoran Đinđić]] was shot dead by a sniper linked to organised crime and former security units in the [[e:Assassination of Zoran Đinđić|2003 assassination]], and the governments that followed became associated with patronage, privatisation scandals and the 2008 financial crash.

That opening was seized by men from Milošević's own camp. In 1998–2000 [[p:Aleksandar Vučić]] had been Milošević's information minister, a hardline member of the nationalist [[p:Serbian Radical Party]]. In 2008 he and [[p:Tomislav Nikolić]] broke away to found the [[p:Serbian Progressive Party]], {{note: Founded on 8 September 2008 by Nikolić and Vučić as a pro-EU split from the Serbian Radical Party.}} recasting themselves as pro-European reformers. The SNS came to power in 2012; Vučić became prime minister in 2014 and president in 2017.

Over the next decade critics, and watchdogs such as Freedom House, described a slide toward a hybrid regime: friendly tabloids and TV channels, pressure on independent media, public jobs tied to party loyalty, and elections that were competitive but tilted. Vučić's supporters pointed instead to growth, foreign investment, big infrastructure projects and a careful balance between the EU, Russia and China. Protest waves came and went, in 2018–19 and after two mass shootings in 2023, but the fragmented opposition parties could never turn them into a majority.

The break came on 1 November 2024, when the newly renovated concrete canopy of Novi Sad's railway station collapsed in the [[e:Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse]], {{note: The canopy fell on 1 November 2024; the death toll eventually reached 16.}} killing 16 people. For many Serbians the renovation, part of a Chinese-built rail project, symbolised a state where contracts mattered more than safety. Students began blockading their faculties that month, and the [[e:2024–present Serbian anti-corruption protests|movement]] spread to farmers, teachers and lawyers. Like Otpor, it refused to have leaders or to merge with the old opposition. Prime minister [[p:Miloš Vučević]] resigned in January 2025, and on 15 March independent counters estimated around 300,000 people in Belgrade, one of the largest rallies in Serbia's history.

The students then made a decisive choice: instead of backing existing parties, they fielded their own slate of professors, doctors and professionals, the Student List. After Vučić stepped down as president in September 2026 to run for prime minister, the snap election of 25 October became a referendum on his era, and the students won 140 of 250 seats on the highest turnout in three decades.

timeline.text: Students in Belgrade found [[p:Otpor]], a leaderless nonviolent movement against Milošević; the same year Vučić becomes his information minister.
Mass protests over a stolen presidential election topple Milošević in the [[e:Overthrow of Slobodan Milošević|Bulldozer Revolution]].
Reformist PM Zoran Đinđić is assassinated in Belgrade, a blow to the post-Milošević reform project.
Vučić and Nikolić found the [[p:Serbian Progressive Party]] as a pro-EU split from the Radicals; it wins power in 2012.
Vučić becomes prime minister (2014), then president (2017); he is re-elected in 2022.
The [[e:Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse]] kills 16 people and sparks student blockades across Serbia.
PM Miloš Vučević resigns; on 15 March an estimated 300,000 people rally in Belgrade.
After Vučić quits the presidency to run for PM, the Student List wins 140 of 250 seats; final results are confirmed on 5 Nov.

perspectives.view: They present their years in power as a period of stability, growth and investment after the chaotic democratic governments of the 2000s, with Serbia steering its own course between the EU, Russia and China. They have often cast the protests as a foreign-backed attempt at a [[e:Colour revolution|colour revolution]] rather than a genuine domestic movement.

perspectives.side: The student movement and its supporters
perspectives.view: They see the Novi Sad collapse as the deadly result of a captured state, where party loyalty and opaque contracts replaced accountability. In their telling, they are finishing the job of 2000, which removed Milošević but not the system of patronage that let his former officials return.

keyTerms.meaning: Srpska napredna stranka, the [[p:Serbian Progressive Party]]; founded in 2008 and in power from 2012 until the 2026 election.
Serbian for 'Resistance!'; the 1998–2000 student movement whose nonviolent tactics helped topple Milošević and were later copied abroad.
The students' main tactic since November 2024: occupying faculties and roads to halt normal life and press their demands for accountability.
A system that holds real elections but tilts the field through control of media, state resources and institutions; the label watchdogs applied to Serbia under the SNS.

items.whyItMatters: The history of 2000 is the warning: a street victory followed by infighting and weak institutions let the old guard return within a decade. Watch whether the leaderless Student List can agree on a prime minister and hold together once the new assembly sits, how it handles the presidential election due by 27 Dec, and whether it reopens the stalled EU accession track while managing Serbia's ties with Russia and China.

items.title: Why Moscow's choice of Medinsky matters: Russia–Ukraine talks from Minsk to Abu Dhabi
items.hook: Russia is sending [[p:Vladimir Medinsky]] to this week's Abu Dhabi talks, and analysts read that as a sign of stalling. The reason lies in a decade of negotiations that keep producing prisoner swaps and local truces, but never a settlement.
items.body:
Russia and Ukraine have been negotiating, on and off, for more than a decade, and the pattern repeats: talks produce humanitarian deals, but never a settlement, because the two sides disagree about what comes first.

The template was set in Donbas. After Russian-backed separatists seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014, the [[e:Minsk agreements]] {{note: Minsk I was signed in September 2014 and Minsk II in February 2015, brokered by France and Germany with Russia and Ukraine.}} promised a ceasefire, local elections and special status for the breakaway areas. They foundered on **sequencing**: Kyiv wanted Russian forces out and its border back before any vote, while Moscow insisted on elections first. Eight years of the [[p:Normandy Format]] {{note: Leaders' grouping of Germany, France, Russia and Ukraine, first convened during D-Day commemorations in Normandy in June 2014.}} never closed that gap. On 21 February 2022 Russia recognised the separatist republics, and Putin declared Minsk dead the next day.

Within days of the [[e:Russian invasion of Ukraine|full-scale invasion]], delegations met in Belarus, and in late March 2022 they reached a draft framework in Istanbul: Ukrainian neutrality in exchange for international security guarantees, with Crimea parked for 15 years. Russia's chief negotiator was [[p:Vladimir Medinsky]] {{note: Russian culture minister from 2012 to 2020 and a presidential aide since 2020; author of popular, nationalist-tinged books on Russian history.}}. Why those [[e:Peace negotiations in the Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)|Istanbul talks]] collapsed is still argued over. Moscow says Western leaders talked Kyiv out of a deal. Ukrainian officials say Russia demanded caps on Ukraine's army and a veto over its guarantees, terms they saw as capitulation, and the discovery of the [[e:Bucha massacre]] after Russia's retreat from Kyiv hardened opinion. Many historians point to several causes at once.

The direct channel stayed closed for three years. When it reopened in Istanbul in May 2025, under pressure from the new Trump administration, Moscow sent Medinsky again. The rounds yielded the war's largest prisoner swaps but no ceasefire; Medinsky reportedly reminded Kyiv that Peter the Great fought Sweden for 21 years, a signal that Russia was prepared to wait.

In 2026 the US moved the talks into a trilateral format brokered by [[p:Steve Witkoff]]. Tellingly, Russia changed its negotiator: the two [[e:2026 United States–Ukraine–Russia meetings in Abu Dhabi|Abu Dhabi rounds]] in January and February were led by the military intelligence chief [[p:Igor Kostyukov]], and produced a 314-prisoner exchange and talk of ceasefire mechanics. When Medinsky returned at [[e:2026 United States–Ukraine–Russia meetings in Geneva|Geneva]] in February, the military track was constructive but the political talks stalled again over Russia's demand for all of Donbas. In March the US–Iran war put the format on pause; prisoner swaps carried on through mediators.

That history explains why the choice of Medinsky for this week's Abu Dhabi round is read as a sign. With him at the table, Russia has tended to restate its full political demands rather than trade on details. Ukraine's lead, [[p:Rustem Umerov]], was in the room with him in Istanbul in 2022 and 2025 and in Geneva.

timeline.text: The [[e:Minsk agreements|Minsk Protocol]] sets out a ceasefire in Donbas; it soon breaks down.
Minsk II, brokered by France and Germany, sets out elections and special status for the separatist areas, but the order of steps is never agreed.
Russia recognises the separatist republics, declares Minsk void and launches the [[e:Russian invasion of Ukraine|full-scale invasion]].
Talks in Istanbul, with [[p:Vladimir Medinsky]] leading Russia's team, produce a draft on neutrality and guarantees; they collapse by May.
Direct talks resume in Istanbul under US pressure, again led by Medinsky. They bring large prisoner swaps but no ceasefire.
US-brokered trilateral rounds in Abu Dhabi, led for Russia by GRU chief [[p:Igor Kostyukov]], bring a prisoner swap; at Geneva in February Medinsky returns and political talks stall.
The US–Iran war puts the trilateral format on pause; prisoner exchanges continue through mediators.
The Oleshky local truce lapses on 1 Nov; talks resume in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 Nov with Medinsky facing [[p:Rustem Umerov]].

perspectives.view: Moscow says Kyiv sabotaged the Minsk agreements and walked away from a near-deal in Istanbul in 2022 under Western pressure. It argues any settlement must address the war's 'root causes': Ukraine's NATO ambitions and the status of territories it now claims.

Kyiv says Russia used Minsk to freeze its occupation of Donbas and offered terms in 2022 that would have left Ukraine disarmed and without real guarantees. It wants a ceasefire on current lines first, and refuses to hand over land Russia has not taken.
Many see no single cause for the 2022 collapse, pointing to disputes over guarantees and army limits, Russian atrocities, and shifts on the battlefield. They disagree on how close a deal really was.

keyTerms.meaning: The 2014 and 2015 deals meant to end the war in Donbas. They failed largely over whether elections or Ukraine regaining its border should come first.
The March 2022 draft framework that traded Ukrainian neutrality for security guarantees from other states. It was never finalised.
US–Russia–Ukraine talks, run since January 2026 with American envoys mediating in the room, rather than the bilateral Istanbul channel.
Ukraine's eastern Donetsk and Luhansk regions. Russia's demand for all of it, including areas Ukraine still holds, is the main sticking point.

items.whyItMatters: Past rounds led by Medinsky have restated Russia's maximal political terms, while rounds led by military officials have produced practical deals such as prisoner swaps and ceasefire mechanics. Watch whether Abu Dhabi yields anything beyond humanitarian steps, such as a renewed local truce, and whether talk of territory moves at all. Washington's push for a broader US–Russia deal could also change what each side thinks it can hold out for.

items.title: How Saudi Arabia and the Houthis became enemies
items.hook: Turkey has ratified the [[e:Mecca Joint Defence Agreement]] and Syrian troops are reportedly heading to the Saudi–Yemeni border, as [[p:Houthis|Houthi]] missiles keep hitting Riyadh. The roots of this war run back to a 1934 border treaty and a religious rivalry in Yemen's northern mountains.
items.body:
The quarrel between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's northern highlands is older than the Houthis. In 1934 [[p:Ibn Saud]]'s new kingdom defeated Yemen's Zaydi imam in the [[e:Saudi–Yemeni war (1934)]] {{note: A short border war fought in spring 1934 between Ibn Saud's forces and Imam Yahya's Kingdom of Yemen.}}. The treaty signed at Taif left **Asir, Jizan and Najran** under Saudi rule, provinces many Yemenis still call lost land. The border was only finally fixed in 2000, and it runs straight past Saada, the Zaydi heartland.

For decades, though, Riyadh was the Zaydi imams' ally, not their enemy. When republican officers overthrew the imamate in 1962, Saudi Arabia armed the royalist tribes against Egyptian-backed republicans in the [[e:North Yemen civil war]] until 1970. The shift came later. From the 1980s, Saudi-funded Salafi preachers built schools in the north, most famously at Dammaj near Saada, and taught that Zaydi traditions were heresy. Zaydi revivalists pushed back. In the 1990s a cleric's son, Hussein al-Houthi, turned that revival into a political movement that denounced the Yemeni government, America, Israel and Saudi influence alike.

The movement became an armed one after Hussein was killed by government troops in 2004. Six rounds of the [[e:Houthi insurgency]] followed in Saada, and in late 2009 the Houthis crossed the frontier. Saudi Arabia went to war against them directly for the first time, losing more than a hundred soldiers in a few months of mountain fighting. Riyadh came away convinced the group was an Iranian proxy on its border, a reading the Houthis rejected as cover for Saudi meddling.

The [[e:Arab Spring]] broke the Yemeni state. In September 2014 the [[p:Houthis]], allied with former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, seized Sanaa. In March 2015 Saudi Arabia, led by its young defence minister [[p:Mohammed bin Salman]], launched the [[e:Saudi-led intervention in the Yemeni civil war|Saudi-led intervention]] to restore the ousted government. Instead of a quick win it became a long war of airstrikes and blockade on one side, and on the other, Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Saudi cities and oil sites, peaking with the [[e:Abqaiq–Khurais attack]] {{note: Drone and missile strike on Saudi Aramco plants on 14 September 2019; the Houthis claimed it, while Washington blamed Iran.}} in 2019.

By 2022 both sides were exhausted. A UN truce in April largely held even after it formally lapsed, and in 2023, after Saudi Arabia and Iran restored relations, Saudi envoys negotiated face to face with the Houthis in Sanaa. A deal seemed close.

The war with Iran ended that. Fighting in Yemen resumed in mid-2026, and the Houthis took their fight back into the kingdom, striking Riyadh's airport and oil infrastructure. This time Riyadh is not leading a coalition of Gulf neighbours but recruiting bigger powers: Egypt's defensive deployment, Turkey's ratification of the [[e:Mecca Joint Defence Agreement]] {{note: Defence pact joining Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey; Turkey completed ratification on 4 November 2026.}} and reported Syrian troops on the border. The ninety-year-old border quarrel has become a regional alliance contest.

timeline.text: Saudi Arabia wins the [[e:Saudi–Yemeni war (1934)]]; the Treaty of Taif leaves Asir, Jizan and Najran under Saudi rule.
Riyadh backs Yemen's Zaydi royalists against Egyptian-backed republicans in the [[e:North Yemen civil war]].
Zaydi revival in Saada, partly a reaction to Saudi-funded Salafi schools, grows into Hussein al-Houthi's movement.
Hussein al-Houthi is killed by Yemeni troops, starting the [[e:Houthi insurgency]].
Houthi fighters cross the border and Saudi Arabia fights them directly for the first time.
After the Houthis take Sanaa, the [[e:Saudi-led intervention in the Yemeni civil war|Saudi-led intervention]] begins.
A UN-brokered truce halts most fighting; Saudi–Houthi talks follow in 2023.
With Yemen's war reignited, Turkey ratifies the [[e:Mecca Joint Defence Agreement]] and Syrian troops are reported on the Saudi–Yemeni border.

perspectives.view: Riyadh sees the [[p:Houthis]] as an Iranian-armed militia that seized Yemen's capital by force and threatens Saudi cities. It frames its campaigns as defending its border and restoring Yemen's recognised government.

The movement presents itself as resisting decades of Saudi interference, from the 1934 annexation of Yemeni provinces to Salafi proselytising and the 2015 war and blockade. It describes its strikes on the kingdom as retaliation against aggression.

perspectives.side: Yemen's government and many Yemenis outside Houthi areas
perspectives.view: They see the Houthis as a coup movement that overthrew a transitional government and imposes rule by one family and sect. Many also blame the Saudi-led air war and blockade for much of the civilian suffering.

keyTerms.meaning: A branch of Shia Islam centred in Yemen's northern highlands, whose imams ruled parts of Yemen for about a thousand years until 1962.
The settlement after the 1934 war that left Asir, Jizan and Najran inside Saudi Arabia; the border was finalised by the Treaty of Jeddah in 2000.
Northern Yemeni province on the Saudi border, heartland of Zaydism and birthplace of the Houthi movement.
"Supporters of God", the Houthi movement's official name.

items.whyItMatters: The [[p:Houthis]] sit on Saudi Arabia's longest land border and next to the Bab al-Mandab strait, so this war threatens Saudi oil, Red Sea shipping and the kingdom's plans to diversify its economy. Because the Houthis read Saudi pressure through ninety years of grievance, outside troops from Egypt, Turkey or Syria may harden their resolve rather than deter them. Watch whether any US–Iran deal over Hormuz also covers Yemen, and whether the 2023 Saudi–Houthi channel reopens.

items.recallA: For most of the 20th century Riyadh had backed Yemen's Zaydi royalists, notably in the 1962–1970 civil war. items.title: How Beijing's pressure on Taiwan grew from shelling islands to rehearsing a blockade
items.hook: Taipei says more than 100 Chinese navy and coast guard ships are around Taiwan, and analysts read undeclared drills led by the [[p:Chinese aircraft carrier Liaoning|Liaoning]] as a rehearsal of isolating the island. Beijing has tried to squeeze Taiwan since 1954; what has changed is the means.
items.body:
When Taiwan's defence ministry reports a hundred Chinese ships around the island, it is describing the latest stage of a contest that began with artillery. In 1949 [[p:Chiang Kai-shek]]'s [[p:Kuomintang]] lost the [[e:Chinese Civil War]] {{note: Fought on and off from 1927 between the Kuomintang-led Republic of China and the Chinese Communist Party; major fighting ended in 1949.}} and moved the Republic of China's government to Taiwan. [[p:Mao Zedong]] planned to finish the job, but the Korean War brought the US Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait in 1950, and the island stayed out of reach.

What Beijing could reach were the small islands hugging its coast. In September 1954 it began shelling Kinmen (Quemoy) and Matsu, opening the [[e:First Taiwan Strait Crisis]]. The result was the opposite of what it wanted: Washington signed a mutual defence treaty with Taipei that December, and in 1955 Congress authorised the president to defend Taiwan. In August 1958 the guns opened up again in the [[e:Second Taiwan Strait Crisis]]; US ships escorted supply convoys, the blockade failed, and the shelling dwindled into a ritual of alternate-day bombardment that lasted two decades.

The pattern of the next crisis was different. By the 1990s Taiwan had become a democracy, and President [[p:Lee Teng-hui]] was pressing for international space. After he spoke at Cornell University in June 1995, the [[p:People's Liberation Army]] fired missiles into waters off Taiwan, and again in March 1996, before the island's first direct presidential election. This was the [[e:Third Taiwan Strait Crisis]]. The United States sent two aircraft-carrier groups, and Beijing, which had no navy able to challenge them, could only watch Lee win. Many analysts trace China's naval build-up of the following decades to that humiliation.

Beijing spent the next quarter-century building the fleet, missiles and coast guard it lacked, and wrote its red lines into law: the 2005 [[e:Anti-Secession Law]] {{note: Passed by China's National People's Congress in March 2005; it authorises "non-peaceful means" if Taiwan moves toward formal independence.}} permits force if peaceful unification becomes impossible.

The new capabilities showed in August 2022. After US House Speaker [[p:Nancy Pelosi]] visited Taipei, the PLA held days of drills in zones ringing the island and fired missiles over it, the [[e:2022 Chinese military exercises around Taiwan]]. Since then large drills have become routine responses to political moments: Tsai Ing-wen's 2023 meeting with the US House Speaker, [[p:Lai Ching-te]]'s inauguration in May 2024 (Joint Sword-2024A, which added coast guard patrols), Strait Thunder in April 2025 and [[e:Justice Mission 2025]] {{note: PLA drills around Taiwan on 29–30 December 2025, focused on blockading the ports of Keelung and Kaohsiung.}} in December 2025. Each has practised encircling Taiwan, cutting off its ports and keeping outside help away.

This month's deployment adds a twist: it was not announced. Taiwanese officials and US analysts read the carrier-led "area denial" activity as a rehearsal of isolation run quietly, weeks before Taiwan's 28 November local elections and Trump's meeting with Xi. Beijing calls it routine training. Seventy years on, the aim of encircling Taiwan has not changed; the tools have.

timeline.text: The Kuomintang loses the [[e:Chinese Civil War]] and moves the Republic of China's government to Taiwan.
PRC shelling of Kinmen and Matsu opens the [[e:First Taiwan Strait Crisis]]; the US signs a defence treaty with Taipei.
The [[e:Second Taiwan Strait Crisis]]: an attempted artillery blockade of Kinmen fails as US ships escort supply convoys.
After [[p:Lee Teng-hui]]'s Cornell visit, PLA missile tests bracket Taiwan's first direct presidential election; the US sends two carrier groups.
China's [[e:Anti-Secession Law]] authorises "non-peaceful means" against formal independence.
After [[p:Nancy Pelosi]]'s Taipei visit, the PLA rings Taiwan with exercise zones and fires missiles over the island.
Named drills (Joint Sword, Strait Thunder, [[e:Justice Mission 2025]]) rehearse blockading Taiwan's ports, now with coast guard ships.
Taipei reports 100+ Chinese ships and undeclared carrier-led "area denial" drills ahead of its 28 Nov local elections.

perspectives.view: Taiwan has been part of China since antiquity and the civil war's division is an internal matter. Its drills are a lawful response to "Taiwan independence" separatists and foreign interference, and Beijing seeks peaceful reunification but will not rule out force.

The [[p:Democratic Progressive Party]] government of [[p:Lai Ching-te]] says the Republic of China (Taiwan) is a sovereign state the PRC has never ruled, and that its future must be decided by its 23 million people; the drills are coercion meant to intimidate voters. The opposition [[p:Kuomintang]] also rejects PRC rule but favours more dialogue with Beijing.

Washington acknowledges Beijing's position under its one-China policy without endorsing it, and under the [[e:Taiwan Relations Act]] supplies Taiwan with defensive arms. It opposes any change to the status quo by force or coercion from either side.

keyTerms.meaning: Taiwan-held island groups a few kilometres off mainland China's coast, the targets of the 1954–55 and 1958 crises.
2005 PRC law permitting "non-peaceful means" if Taiwan moves toward formal independence or peaceful unification becomes impossible.
Military operations aimed at keeping an adversary's forces out of a zone; around Taiwan, at keeping US and allied help away.
1979 US law, passed after Washington switched recognition to Beijing, that keeps unofficial ties with Taiwan and provides for its defensive arms.

items.whyItMatters: Each crisis since 1954 has shown Beijing what it lacked, and the PLA now has the ships to practise encircling Taiwan rather than just shelling its islands. Undeclared drills blur the line between exercise and real deployment, which shortens warning time. Watch whether pressure rises around the 28 Nov local elections, and whether Taiwan comes up when [[p:Donald Trump]] meets [[p:Xi Jinping]] at APEC on 18–19 Nov.

items.prevQuestion: Why was Saudi Arabia's war with the Houthis in 2009 a turning point compared with the decades before?
items.prevAnswer: For most of the 20th century Riyadh had backed Yemen's Zaydi royalists, notably in the 1962–1970 civil war. In 2009 it fought the Zaydi-rooted Houthis directly for the first time, after they crossed the border, and came away seeing them as an Iranian proxy, a view that shaped its 2015 intervention.
items.recallQ: Why did the 1995–96 Taiwan Strait crisis push China to build a much larger navy?
items.recallA: Beijing fired missiles near Taiwan to deter voters from backing Lee Teng-hui, but when the US sent two aircraft-carrier groups, the PLA had no way to challenge them and Lee won anyway. Many analysts see that humiliation as a driver of the naval, missile and coast-guard build-up that now lets China rehearse encircling the island.

items.title: How Ethiopia and Eritrea went from comrades to enemies, allies and enemies again
items.hook: Ethiopia told the UN Horn of Africa envoy that Eritrea and Sudan arm rebels inside its borders; Eritrea has denied backing them. The charge flips the alliance of 2018–2022, when Eritrean troops fought for Addis Ababa against the [[p:Tigray People's Liberation Front|TPLF]].
items.body:
Ethiopia's complaint to the UN that Eritrea arms rebels on its soil is the latest turn in a relationship that has swung from comradeship to war, to alliance, and back to open hostility. The two countries share languages, churches and the Tigrinya-speaking highlands, but a century of separate history pulls them apart.

That history began when Italy proclaimed the colony of Eritrea in 1890. Britain took it over in 1941, and in 1952 the UN joined it to [[p:Haile Selassie]]'s Ethiopia as an autonomous unit in a federation. The emperor wore that autonomy down, and in 1962 the Eritrean assembly, under heavy pressure, voted the federation away. Eritreans call this an annexation. Many Ethiopians saw it as reuniting the old highland kingdom with its coast. An armed revolt led by the [[p:Eritrean Liberation Front]] had already begun in 1961, opening the thirty-year [[e:Eritrean War of Independence]].

The war outlasted the emperor. After the [[p:Derg]] {{note: Military committee that overthrew Haile Selassie in 1974, led by Mengistu Haile Mariam until its fall in 1991.}} seized power, two rebel movements fought it: the [[p:Eritrean People's Liberation Front]] {{note: Formed in the early 1970s by fighters who split from the Eritrean Liberation Front; renamed the PFDJ in 1994.}} and the [[p:Tigray People's Liberation Front]] {{note: Founded in 1975 in Tigray by student activists; it led the coalition that ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018.}}. They were allies of necessity, and they quarrelled in the 1980s over strategy and ideology. In May 1991 they won together: Eritrean fighters took Asmara, and a TPLF-led coalition took Addis Ababa. Ethiopia's new leader, [[p:Meles Zenawi]], accepted Eritrea's right to leave. After a 1993 referendum Eritrea became independent, and Ethiopia lost its coast.

The friendship broke over trade, currency and a border no one had marked on the ground. In May 1998 a clash at Badme grew into the [[e:Eritrean–Ethiopian War]], a trench war that killed tens of thousands. The [[e:Algiers Agreement (2000)|Algiers Agreement]] set up a boundary commission, which in 2002 placed Badme in Eritrea. Ethiopia refused to withdraw. Two decades of "no war, no peace" followed, which [[p:Isaias Afwerki]] used to justify open-ended national service and the absence of elections.

[[p:Abiy Ahmed]] broke the deadlock in 2018 by accepting the ruling, and the [[e:2018 Eritrea–Ethiopia summit]] earned him the Nobel Peace Prize. The thaw was also a pact against a shared rival, the TPLF. When the [[e:Tigray war]] {{note: Fought from November 2020 between Ethiopia's federal government and the TPLF; ended by an agreement signed in Pretoria in November 2022.}} broke out, Eritrean troops fought beside federal forces, and rights groups accused them of massacres. But Eritrea was left out of the 2022 peace deal, and in 2023 Abiy called access to the Red Sea an existential question for Ethiopia. Asmara heard a threat to its port of Assab.

By 2026 the alliances had flipped. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara in October, and Eritrea cut ties. Addis Ababa now accuses Eritrea of invading and of backing the TPLF-led rebels, its bitterest enemy only four years ago. Asmara denies backing them and says Ethiopia wants Assab. Alliances in this rivalry have always formed around a shared enemy, while the core questions of the border, the sea and Tigray's place have never been settled.

timeline.text: The UN federates the former Italian colony of Eritrea with Ethiopia as an autonomous unit.
An armed revolt begins; Haile Selassie ends the federation and makes Eritrea a province, opening the [[e:Eritrean War of Independence]].
Eritrean and Tigrayan rebels topple the [[p:Derg]]; Eritrea votes for independence and Ethiopia becomes landlocked.
A clash at Badme becomes the [[e:Eritrean–Ethiopian War]]; a 2002 boundary ruling gives Badme to Eritrea, and Ethiopia refuses to withdraw.
[[p:Abiy Ahmed]] accepts the ruling, and the [[e:2018 Eritrea–Ethiopia summit]] ends the state of war.
Eritrean troops fight alongside federal forces in the [[e:Tigray war]] but are left out of the 2022 peace deal.
Ethiopia closes its embassy in Asmara and Eritrea cuts ties as a TPLF-led alliance fights the federal government; Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of invading.
Ethiopia tells the UN envoy that Eritrea and Sudan arm rebels on its soil.

perspectives.view: Ethiopia sees the loss of its coast in 1993 as a historical mistake made without regard for its people's needs, and calls Red Sea access an existential question it wants to settle peacefully. It accuses Eritrea of invading the north and colluding with the TPLF.

Eritrea says it won its independence in a thirty-year struggle against an illegal annexation, and that the 2002 boundary ruling settled the border. It reads Ethiopia's talk of sea access as a threat to its sovereignty and its port of Assab, and denies backing the TPLF.

The TPLF stresses its part in defeating the Derg and argues that Abiy and Isaias allied in 2018 to crush Tigray. It holds Eritrean troops responsible for atrocities during the 2020–22 war and says Tigray's autonomy was never restored after the peace deal.

keyTerms.meaning: A small border town whose disputed ownership sparked the 1998–2000 war; the 2002 boundary ruling placed it in Eritrea.
Eritrea's southern Red Sea port, once Ethiopia's main outlet to the sea, and the focus of Eritrean fears about Ethiopia's sea-access ambitions.
The panel set up under the [[e:Algiers Agreement (2000)|Algiers Agreement]]; its 2002 ruling was binding, but Ethiopia refused to implement it until 2018.
The armed standoff of 2000–2018, with closed borders, troops dug in on both sides and rivalries carried into Somalia.

items.whyItMatters: Ethiopia and Eritrea have fought one full-scale war and backed opposite sides in others, and the old disputes over the border and the sea are live again while fighting continues in Tigray. Watch whether Ethiopia brings its charges to the UN Security Council or the African Union, whether Eritrean troops stay inside Tigray, and whether Addis Ababa's rows with Sudan and Eritrea merge into one regional war.

items.title: Why Somalia keeps fighting over when its leaders' terms end
items.hook: Somalia's Supreme Court ruled President [[p:Hassan Sheikh Mohamud]]'s term extension unlawful, and federal forces then took over the court. It is the second mandate crisis in five years, rooted in a 2012 constitution that left the rules for elections and federal power unfinished.
items.body:
Somalia's Supreme Court ruling against President [[p:Hassan Sheikh Mohamud]]'s extended term, and the government's answer of sending troops into the courthouse, is the latest round of a fight that recurs at almost every Somali election: who decides when a mandate ends, and under which rules.

The roots lie in collapse. When [[p:Siad Barre]]'s military regime fell in January 1991, the central state fell with it. The [[e:Somali Civil War]] split the country among clan militias; the northwest declared itself Somaliland, and in 1998 the northeast set up Puntland as an autonomous state. Talks in Arta, Djibouti, in 2000 produced the [[p:Transitional National Government of Somalia|Transitional National Government]] {{note: Formed at the Arta conference in Djibouti in 2000; its authority barely reached beyond parts of Mogadishu.}} and a power-sharing rule known as **4.5**: equal shares for the four largest clan families and half a share for all minority groups combined. Talks in Kenya then created the [[p:Transitional Federal Government of Somalia|Transitional Federal Government]] in 2004, on a charter that promised the regions their own governments.

It was weak and long kept out of the capital. In 2006 the [[p:Islamic Courts Union]] took Mogadishu, Ethiopian troops drove it out, and its militant youth wing became [[p:Al-Shabaab (militant group)|al-Shabaab]] {{note: Grew out of the Islamic Courts' youth militia in the mid-2000s and formally joined al-Qaeda in 2012.}}. African Union troops kept the transitional government alive. On 1 August 2012 a constituent assembly adopted a **Provisional Constitution**, and a new [[p:Federal Parliament of Somalia|federal parliament]] elected Hassan Sheikh president for the first time. The word "provisional" mattered: how power and revenue are split between Mogadishu and the federal member states, the electoral system and the status of the capital were all left to be settled later, by consensus.

Without one-person-one-vote elections, every vote since has been indirect: clan elders pick delegates, delegates pick MPs, and MPs pick the president. Each round needs a political deal between Mogadishu and the states, and each deadline invites a fight. The sharpest came in 2021. [[p:Mohamed Abdullahi Farmajo]] {{note: Former prime minister (2010–11), elected president by parliament in February 2017.}} saw his term expire in February without an agreed vote, and in April the lower house extended his mandate by two years. Rival army units took up positions in Mogadishu, and within weeks parliament dropped the extension and the indirect process resumed. It returned Hassan Sheikh to power in the [[e:2022 Somali presidential election]].

Back in office, he set out to finish the constitution and replace clan selection with universal suffrage. In March 2024 parliament amended the first chapters, which also let the president appoint the prime minister on his own; Puntland withdrew its recognition of the federal government the next day, and Jubaland broke with Mogadishu late that year. In March 2026 lawmakers approved a revised constitution with five-year terms applied to sitting officeholders, pushing elections due in May back by a year. The opposition Somali Future Council, Puntland and Jubaland call the 2012 text the only legitimate one.

The court's 5 November ruling sided with that reading. By taking over the building and installing a new chief justice, the government has turned a legal dispute into a test of who controls the capital, much as in 2021, while foreign mediators try to steer both sides back to a deal.

timeline.text: [[p:Siad Barre]]'s regime falls; the central state collapses and Somaliland declares independence.
The Arta conference in Djibouti forms a transitional government and the 4.5 clan power-sharing formula.
The [[p:Transitional Federal Government of Somalia|Transitional Federal Government]] is formed in Kenya on a federal charter.
A constituent assembly adopts the Provisional Constitution; parliament elects Hassan Sheikh Mohamud president.
Parliament extends [[p:Mohamed Abdullahi Farmajo]]'s expired term by two years; army factions clash and the extension is dropped within weeks.
Constitutional amendments restore universal suffrage and strengthen the presidency; Puntland withdraws recognition of Mogadishu.
A revised constitution sets five-year terms for sitting officeholders, delaying elections due in May by a year.
The Supreme Court rules the extension unlawful; federal forces take over the court and a new chief justice is installed.

perspectives.view: President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud presents the 2024 and 2026 changes as finally completing a constitution left unfinished since 2012 and ending clan-based selection in favour of direct elections, which have not been held nationally since 1969. It rejected the court ruling and says the new constitution now applies.

The opposition Somali Future Council and the leaders of Puntland and Jubaland say the amendments were pushed through unilaterally by a parliament whose own mandate was ending, when the 2012 text requires consensus on the federal settlement. They see the extension as a repeat of 2021 and back the court's call for an election deal.

keyTerms.meaning: Power-sharing rule from the 2000 Arta talks giving equal shares to the four largest clan families (Darod, Hawiye, Dir, Rahanweyn) and half a share to minority groups combined.
Somalia's governing text since 1 August 2012; it set up a federal parliamentary republic but left the division of powers and the electoral system to later negotiation.
The regional governments, among them Puntland, Jubaland, Hirshabelle, Galmudug and South West, whose cooperation every national election has needed.
Somalia's system since 2012: clan elders choose delegates, delegates choose MPs, and parliament elects the president.

items.whyItMatters: Because no election can happen without a deal between Mogadishu and the federal member states, a president who extends his own term without one splits the country's already fragile institutions. Watch the mediated talks set for 14–18 November, whether the opposition goes ahead with parallel elections, and whether the clan uprising in Hirshabelle and Uganda's troop withdrawal open space for [[p:Al-Shabaab (militant group)|al-Shabaab]].

items.recallQ: What is Somalia's 4.5 formula, and why does President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud want to replace the system built on it?
items.recallA: It is the clan power-sharing rule from the 2000 Arta talks: equal shares for the four largest clan families and half a share for minorities, used to fill parliament through clan elders and delegates.
